title: Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence
research_question: Do consumers respond differently to commodity taxes depending on whether the tax is included in the posted price they see while shopping versus added only at the register? How does such differential responsiveness affect the incidence and efficiency cost of taxation?
data_description: The study combines two datasets. The first is weekly product-level scanner data from a national grocery chain covering one treatment store and two nearby control stores in Northern California, spanning week 1 of 2005 through week 13 of 2006. Variables include weekly quantity sold, revenue, and prices for roughly 750 treated toiletry products (cosmetics, hair care accessories, deodorants) and 95 categories of control toiletries. A complementary survey of 91 grocery customers and 49 students measures knowledge of sales tax rates and tax-inclusive price computation. The second dataset is annual state-level data on per-capita beer consumption from the NIAAA from 1970 to 2003, merged with state beer excise tax rates, state sales tax rates, alcohol regulations (drinking age, drunk driving laws), state population, per-capita income, and unemployment. The unit of observation is state-year. ACCRA cost-of-living surveys provide posted beer prices for a subset of years.
institutional_context: In most US retail stores, shelf prices exclude the local sales tax, which is added only at the register; in the Northern California grocery store studied, a 7.375% sales tax applies to roughly 30% of products (including toiletries but excluding most food). Researchers worked with store managers to attach additional shelf tags showing tax-inclusive prices for cosmetics, hair-care accessories, and deodorants over a three-week period in early 2006, while leaving original pretax tags intact and leaving other taxable categories and nearby stores unchanged. The alcohol setting exploits the fact that US states levy two distinct taxes on beer: a state excise tax imposed at wholesale and embedded in the posted shelf or menu price, and a state sales tax added at checkout. Between 1970 and 2003, states changed both tax rates frequently and largely independently, alongside changes in alcohol-related regulations, providing variation in the visibility of tax components facing consumers.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treatment = stores with visible tax, control = stores without visible tax; shock/instrument/cutoff = implementation of tax visibility

key_variables.treatment: visibility of sales tax on price tags
key_variables.control: stores without visible sales tax on price tags
key_variables.time_period: several months before and after the intervention

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Making sales taxes more visible to consumers leads to a reduction in the quantity of goods purchased.
